section.title: Overview
section.para: Scaly is a programming language designed to be self-scaling: it adapts to the needs of the developer, from simple scripts to complex systems. The language combines a uniform grammar — with no hardcoded operators, since operators are ordinary identifiers — with optional region-based memory management. An operation is read from left to right, the type of the value in hand saying what comes next; how strongly operators bind is stated by the standard library, not by the compiler, and parentheses give explicit control where it is needed.

listitem.para: Uniform syntax — Operators are ordinary identifiers rather than keywords baked into the grammar, so the language and its standard library share one small, regular syntax.

Safety without ceremony — Memory is managed through regions the compiler infers, and an escape checker proves at compile time that no reference outlives its memory; ordinary code carries no annotations.
Incremental complexity — Simple programs stay simple; advanced features are available when needed.

section.title: A Language Still Changing
section.para: Scaly is below version 1.0, and it is still changing. Its syntax, its rules and its standard library move where something better is found — recently the assignment became :=, and the precedence table of the compiler gave way to the binding strengths the standard library declares. A version below 1.0 promises nothing about the next one.

What stays is a version that is out. A published toolchain and a published package do not change afterwards, so a program can go on using the ones it was written with: the toolchain by its number (), a package by the version it declares ().
